newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Gold - High prices seen knocking demand.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - High prices seen knocking demand.

text.p: Demand for gold in Asia could soften in coming weeks as India fills its need for the yellow metal ahead of the October festival of lights and other buyers grow price-averse, dealers said on Friday.
Indian buying of gold kilobars was particularly robust, with overall demand steady, a bank trader in Singapore said.
Demand in the lead-up to India's October Diwali festival was expected to remain strong, with a good monsoon expected to boost disposable income, dealers said.
However, a Hong Kong dealer said those factors could not be relied on to support gold prices over the long term.
"India has been buying a lot and it has increased a lot, but this buying will have to stop once they have enough," she said.
Jitters about regional currency problems were also keeping Southeast Asian buyers out of gold, dealers said.
Prices, which have recovered in recent weeks from 12-month lows, were now perceived to be too high for buyers spooked by declines in regional currencies, they said.
At midday on Friday, Hong Kong gold was quoted slightly firmer at US$324.30/80 an ounce, up from its opening price of US$323.70/324.20 and New York's $324.20/324.70.
A Hong Kong bank dealer said he saw gold testing the downside next week at $321.50, with a tail-off in Asian demand and a regrouping by producers who missed this week's highs.
Funds had done their best to push the resistance level of $330, he said, each time seeing it fall back just this side on heavy selling.
"We tried about five times this week," he said, adding that the range of $325-329 that dominated the week's trade was maintained by equity liquidation amid shaky financial markets.
"When it got down to $317 there was no further fresh selling, everyone was holding back," the other Hong Kong source said.
Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam had stepped back, a Singapore trader said.
"When we get to these levels, we see some slackening in demand," he said.
But another trader said investor nervousness in some Southeast Asian nations could prompt buyers to pick up gold as "as a good hedge against all these falling currencies".
Singapore dealers polled by Reuters said they saw gold staying in a range in the coming week, with more near-term testing of the $330 upside probable.
One source pegged spot gold to range between $326 and $329.

"Other people are saying gold will eventually fall to $300 by year-end. But in the short-term, I don't see any reason to sell gold down especially with seasonal demand now coming back," a bank dealer said.
Singapore gold premiums were quoted slightly easier at 65-70 cents per ounce over London spot prices, from 70-75 cents last week.
Hong Kong premiums were seen steady at 100 cents over spot.
